 Amici  are the Major Cities Chiefs Association, the
Police Executive Research Forum, and the United
States Conference of Mayors.
 The Major Cities Chiefs Association (“MCCA”) is a
professional organization of police executives
representing the largest cities in the United States
and Canada.  The mission of MCCA is to provide a
forum for police executives from large population
centers to address the ch allenges and issues of
policing, to influence national and international
policy that affects police services, and to enhance the
development of current and future police leaders.   In
2018, the MCCA formally adopted, through
membership vote, a Firearms Violence Policy that
advocates for “reinstat[ing] the assault weapons
ban….”2

 As the officials most responsible for protecting the
safety of the communi ties they serve, amici
understand that unfettered access to assault-style
weapons like the AR-15 poses a grave public safety
threat to the nation.  Regulations that ban the
possession of these weapons are crucial to securing
public safety, protecting law enforcement officers, and
preventing malign actors fr om readily obtaining the
lethal firearms they use to commit acts of terror and
political violence.  Amici have a strong interest in the
regulation of assault weapons to prevent those who
would wield them from endangering community
members, law enforcement officers, and civic
engagement.
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF
ARGUMENT
 Amici here—chiefs of police and city mayors—are
the public officials most responsible for ensuring the
safety and security of the communities they serve.
They communicate safety information, respond to
threats, calm the public, investigate crimes, and
prosecute offenders.  Law enforcement officials, in
particular, are the first line of defense when a threat
arises—they respond to the scene, control or
eliminate the threat, collect evidence, and provide aid
to those injured or threatened.  Their job is to make
people feel safe and they of ten do so at risk to their
own lives.  This is especially so when law enforcement
responds to a scene where a shooter wields an assaultstyle weapon.  These weapons are inherently
dangerous: they are military-grade weapons designed
to cause enormous harm in short periods of time.  Law
enforcement officers who encounter shooters armed

4
with these weapons are often out-gunned and underprotected from the threat they pose.
 As local public officials, we have watched as the
incidences of mass shootings in our communities rise.
We have watched as our churches, grocery stores,
neighborhoods, office buildings, and schools become
targets for shooters wielding  assault weapons.  We
have watched our teachers, neighbors, pastors, office
workers, and children die fr om gunfire.  We have
watched as political violence has chilled civic
engagement and the exercise of constitutional rights.
And we have watched our law enforcement officers
struggle to respond to the unique, dangerous threat
posed by assault weapons, and sometimes suffer

responsibility to our communities to protect our
constituents from these threats, a responsibility each
of us takes seriously.  We have a duty to do more than
watch.
 Local governments and law enforcement have long
been required—and empowered—to solve novel
problems across a host of issue areas.  See Ariz. State
Legis. v. Ariz. Indep. Redistricting Comm’n, 576 U.S.
787, 817 (2015) (recognizing “the role of the States as
laboratories for devising solutions to difficult legal
problems” (internal quotation marks and citation
omitted)).  Local governments must innovate to “deal

5
with pressing social, economic, and environmental
concerns.”5
 Few problems underscore the need for regulatory
innovation like the increasing availability of assaultstyle weapons.  In New York State Rifle & Pistol
Association v. Bruen , 597 U.S. 1 (2022), this Court
preserved a degree of flexibility for local governments
to protect their constituents.  Bruen reaffirmed that
our Nation has a “historical tradition of prohibiting
the carrying of ‘dangerous and unusual weapons.’”
Bruen, 597 U.S. at 21 (quoting District of Columbia v.
Heller, 554 U.S. 570, 627 (2008 )).  As this Court
reaffirmed recently, the Second Amendment is “‘not a
right to keep and carry any weapon whatsoever in any
manner whatsoever and for whatever purpose.’”
United States v. Rahimi , 602 U.S. 680, 691 (2024)
(quoting Heller, 554 U.S. at 626).  Indeed, since the
Founding, states have banned a range of weapons,
from clubs and Bowie knives to multi-shot firearms
and machine guns.
 Cook County’s Ordinance and the two Connecticut
Acts at issue fit comfortably within Bruen’s tradition
of regulation.  The Second Amendment is not “a
regulatory straightjacket.”  597 U.S. at 30. As the
Second Circuit explained, particularly dangerous
weapons like assault-style rifles that are not
commonly used for self-defense are unprotected by
the Second Amendment, and state and local
governments may prohibit them.  See Nat’l Ass’n for

bans on assault weapons are just such regulatory

not preclude sensible public safety measures that are
well within the historical tradition of regulating
dangerous or unusual weapons.  Without this
latitude, our local governments and police will be
paralyzed in the face of a growing epidemic of gun
violence, and our communities will suffer the harms.

ARGUMENT
I. Mass Shootings Using Assault-Style Weapons
Are an Increasing Threat to Our
Communities.
Mass shootings were essentially unknown for the
first two centuries of the Nation’s history.  According
to expert evidence introduced in cases challenging
regulatory bans, the first mass shooting in America
resulting in double-digit fatalities did not occur until
1949. See Oregon Firearms Fed’n, Inc. v. Brown , 644
F.Supp.3d 782, 803 (D. Or. 2022); Declaration of Louis
Klarevas ¶16, Wiese v. Bonta , No. 2:17-cv-00903-
WBS-CSK (E.D. Cal. Aug. 18, 2023), ECF No. 135-13
(“Klarevas Decl.”).  This shooting was followed by a
second similar incident in 1966, a third in 1975, and
a fourth in 1982.  See  Klarevas Decl. ¶17.  In other
words, these tragedies were initially non-existent,
and then occurred roughly once a decade.
The frequency and intensity of mass shootings
have increased exponentially.  Whereas the first four
mass shootings resulting in ten or more deaths
occurred over more than three decades, the same
number of double-digit killings took place in the two
years of 2022 and 2023 alone.8  These included, within
ten days, the racially motivated killing of ten Black

Mass shootings, defined as when “four or more
people are shot or killed in a single incident, not
including the shooter,” now occur more than daily.10
In 2026, as of October 26, there have been 387 mass

injured.11
In recent years, mass shootings are particularly
